summary:
What we built. TerraTunes is a web app that turns NASA Earth maps into music. Pick a “record” from an illustrated jukebox, each one a real NASA dataset like sea surface temperature, rainfall, or air pollution, and drop the needle. A playhead sweeps the map from west to east, and every value it reads becomes a note: higher values play higher, and extremes play louder.

The problem. NASA’s Earth Information Center publishes some of the clearest pictures of our changing planet, but they are only pictures. People who are blind or have low vision can’t use them, and for everyone else a color map is easy to glance at and hard to feel.

How it answers the challenge. The challenge asks for an Earth Information Jukebox that pairs NASA visualizations with sonifications made from those same visualizations, with accessibility at its core. TerraTunes converts nine NASA visualizations into calibrated numbers, turns them into music through fixed, documented rules, and explains every note.

Who it helps. Blind and low-vision users get an equal way into NASA Earth data through sound, keyboard controls, and screen-reader text. Students, teachers, and museum visitors get a second sense for the same data: hearing where the oceans run hot or where storms pour down makes climate patterns memorable.
details: TerraTunes: The Earth Information Jukebox turns nine NASA Earth datasets (temperature, wind, precipitation, air quality, sea surface temperature, and vegetation) into music you can play, explore, and verify. Drop the needle on a record and the app extracts frames from the NASA movie, calibrates each pixel against its color bar into physical units, and applies fixed, deterministic rules that map west-to-east position to pitch, averages and extremes to loudness, spatial variation to rhythm, and change over time to tempo, with missing-data regions left silent. Users can choose Orchestra, Clear tone, or Musical sound, explore in Scan, Overview, or Explore modes, trace any note back to its source measurement in the Data Deck, scan their own images, or download MP3/WAV soundscapes. Built with React, TypeScript, the Web Audio API, and a Python/FastAPI backend, TerraTunes gives blind and low-vision users a first-class, keyboard- and screen-reader-friendly way into NASA Earth science, while helping students, teachers, and museum visitors remember climate patterns through sound. It pairs the warmth of a vintage jukebox with honest sonification (real calibrated values, never invented data) and transparently discloses its use of Manus, Seedance, and Claude Code.
